e: Fabiola (Nicholas Wiseman, 1854)

Cardinal Wiseman's novel is set in the Rome of Diocletian and Maximian, during the great persecution of the Christians that began in 303, and ends with the victory of Constantine. Its heroine is Fabiola, a rich pagan Roman girl who is baptized by the end of the novel. Beside her, the Roman martyrs of Christian tradition are the main characters: Pancratius, Sebastian and Agnes.

This is a literary walk: it follows the plot of the novel, not a historical account. The novel takes the martyrs' stories from late antique acts of the martyrs and from legend; their historical value is limited. Wiseman was also an archaeologist, and he often gives the places precisely, citing the excavations of his own day. The novel has three parts; references give the part and chapter number. The text follows the English edition on Project Gutenberg.
Lucina's house

The novel opens on a September afternoon in the Campus Martius. According to the novel, the house of Lucina, the Christian widow, stood exactly opposite the east side of the Saepta Iulia: the church of San Marcello stands on its grounds today, and it reached back to the foot of the Quirinal (Part I, chapter 1).

Here Lucina talks with her fourteen-year-old son Pancratius. That day at school the oldest pupil, Corvinus, challenged Pancratius to a fight; he refused to fight, so Corvinus struck him in the face. Lucina therefore decides the time has come: she gives her son the little purse she wears around her neck, holding a sponge stained with the blood of his martyred father (Part I, chapters 2–3).

San Marcello is one of Rome's titular churches. According to the Liber Pontificalis, Pope Marcellus was condemned, as a punishment, to serve as a stable hand in his church, which stood in the house of a woman named Lucina; the novel's Lucina alludes to this tradition.
The Vicus Patricius: Agnes's house and the pope's church

According to the novel, Agnes, Fabiola's Christian cousin, twelve or thirteen years old, lived with her parents on the Vicus Patricius. On the same street stood the house of the senator Pudens, where according to tradition the Apostle Peter also lived, and which in the time of the novel was the church and residence of the popes (Part II, chapter 10). Here the pope consecrates Agnes and Syra, Fabiola's slave, as brides of Christ. The blind Caecilia joins them as a third, bringing a crown woven of thorns instead of flowers (Part II, chapter 11).

According to the novel, Fabiola's family lived in the house of Fabius, a knight, in the valley between the Quirinal and the Esquiline (Part I, chapter 4); it gives no more precise location.

The novel itself identifies the Vicus Patricius by the church of Santa Pudenziana; the church stands on the site of the titulus Pudentis, and its apse mosaic was made around 400. The tradition of the house of Pudens and of Peter's stay there is legendary.
Sebastian's apartment on the Palatine

Sebastian, a Christian officer of the imperial guard, lives on the Palatine. The novel describes the place precisely: in the rooms named after Mammaea, built by Alexander Severus, at the corner of the hill that looks toward the Caelian, above the later Arch of Constantine and the Meta Sudans fountain (Part I, chapter 9).

On a moonlit autumn evening Sebastian and Pancratius look out from here at the Flavian amphitheater, the Septizodium and the Baths of Caracalla. Pancratius points to the arches of the amphitheater: their triumphal arch is there. Then a lion's roar is heard from below the Caelian; wild beasts have been brought to the amphitheater's vivarium.

The Historia Augusta does mention rooms on the Palatine named after Mammaea (Alexander Severus 26); their location is unknown. The stop is the Meta Sudans fountain, which the novel also names.
The cemetery of Callistus on the Via Appia

Diogenes, the old gravedigger, lives with his sons in the Subura and is the chief gravedigger of the cemetery of Callistus (Part II, chapters 1–2). The faithful set out in pairs along the Via Appia, and nearly two miles from the gate, behind the tombs, they go down through different entrances of a villa. Diogenes leads the young people through the galleries with a lamp; Torquatus secretly draws marks in the sand so that he can find his way back later (Part II, chapters 2–4).

The apostate Torquatus, recruited by Fulvius, the informer, betrays the cemetery. After the edict is proclaimed, soldiers break in. They capture Caecilia, the blind Christian girl, who dies quietly, without violence, before the prefect's tribunal (Part II, chapters 16–17).

The catacomb of Callistus lies along the Via Appia Antica, beyond the edge of the map; the stop is the Porta Appia. The crypt of the 3rd-century popes was uncovered by Giovanni Battista de Rossi around 1854; he is the novel's “young antiquarian.”
The Baths of Caracalla

The Baths of Caracalla are one of the main meeting places of the novel's pagan Rome. In the gaming hall of the baths Torquatus, the dubious Christian, loses his money. Fulvius, the informer, keeps him in his power by threatening to denounce him if he returns to the Christians (Part II, chapter 9).

The baths' cloakroom keeper, the Christian Cucumio, and his wife Victoria watch the meetings of the three. Victoria overhears the plan to raid the cemetery of Callistus on the day after the proclamation, and warns the Christians in time (Part II, chapters 15–16).

The Baths of Caracalla were dedicated in 216. The novel also alludes to Cucumio's epitaph.
The edict in the Forum

Corvinus nails up the imperial edict on the extermination of the Christians in the Forum, on a board fixed to a pillar near the Puteal Libonis, the magistrate's seat. At night Dacian guards watch the square (Part II, chapter 13).

Pancratius and the centurion Quadratus nevertheless tear it down and burn the pieces in Diogenes's house in the Subura. In the morning Corvinus finds only the empty board, and on the ground a knife he had seen in the hands of a schoolmate (Part II, chapters 13–14).

The story repeats in Rome an event at Nicomedia involving Diocletian's first edict of 303: according to Lactantius, a Christian tore it down and ripped it up there (De mortibus persecutorum 13). The exact location of the Puteal Libonis is disputed; the stop is the Rostra.
The building of the Baths of Diocletian

Early in the novel, at Fabius's banquet, there is talk that the emperor wants his baths finished within three years and is having convicts brought here from the mines of the empire (Part I, chapter 6). After the edict the work grows even crueler: the baths are built by Christian prisoners (Part II, chapter 20).

Corvinus picks fighters from among them for the games. The superintendent of the convicts leads him around the building site; according to the novel, the round vestibule lit from above is like that of the Pantheon.

The Baths of Diocletian were completed around 305. The tradition that they were built by Christian convicts comes from late antique acts of the martyrs and medieval legends; no contemporary source confirms it.

Pancratius, with twenty companions, is driven in chains through the streets to the Mamertine prison, beaten along the way, and thrust down into the lower chamber. The novel describes the two underground chambers one above the other, connected only by a round opening in the middle of the vault (Part II, chapter 21). The sentence: they are to be thrown to the wild beasts in the Flavian amphitheater.

Later Agnes too is locked in this prison, in the novel's word the “Tullianum,” on Fulvius's accusation. Fabiola learns of it from a guard, goes in to her, and speaks with her for the last time before the execution (Part II, chapters 28–29).

This is the map's real Carcer: its lower, round chamber is the Tullianum.
The death of Pancratius in the amphitheater

On a frosty morning the crowd streams into the Flavian amphitheater; the emperor sits in the imperial box on the east side (Part II, chapter 23). Pancratius stands motionless, facing the emperor. A panther is let loose on him and with one spring tears open his throat. Pancratius's blood mingles with his father's in the purse he wears around his neck.

At the end of the novel Corvinus, who betrayed Pancratius, wanders drunk to the wild-beast cages beside the amphitheater, and a panther kills him the same way, through the bars (Part III, chapter 2).

According to tradition, the real Pancratius was not killed by wild beasts but beheaded on the Via Aurelia.
The tomb of Pancratius on the Via Aurelia

Pancratius's body is buried along the Via Aurelia in the cemetery that later took his name, and that passed the name on to the neighboring gate (Part II, chapter 24). The novel adds that in times of peace a basilica was built over his tomb, which still stands.

The basilica and catacomb of San Pancrazio are indeed behind the Janiculum, along the Via Aurelia. The Porta Aurelia is known today as Porta San Pancrazio.
The martyrdom of Sebastian on the Palatine

Sebastian is betrayed. On the orders of the emperor Maximian, the palace's Mauritanian archers shoot him with arrows one dawn. According to the novel, an old chapel among the ruins of the Palatine marks the spot where he fell (Part II, chapter 25).

But Sebastian survives: he is carried to the apartment of Irene, a Christian lady living on the Palatine, where Dionysius, priest and physician, tends him. After his recovery he confronts the emperor on the palace's great staircase, and the emperor has him clubbed to death before his eyes and his body thrown into the Cloaca Maxima. Lucina finds it and buries it where Sebastian's basilica now stands on the Via Appia (Part II, chapters 26–27).

The novel follows Sebastian's late antique acts. The chapel is San Sebastiano al Palatino, in the Vigna Barberini; the stop is the excavated temple next to it, believed to be Elagabalus's.
The martyrdom of Agnes

Fulvius, the informer, whom Agnes had once turned down, denounces her as a Christian, and the prefect condemns her. Of the first part of her sentence the novel says nothing, except that her angel protected her and her presence turned the “den of infamy” into a sanctuary. According to the footnote, this place is marked by the church of Sant'Agnese on the Piazza Navona (Part II, chapter 29).

Early the next morning she is brought before the prefect again in the Forum. The manacles slip from her thin wrists. Agnes kneels, draws her hair forward, and the executioner beheads her with a single stroke of the sword.

Sant'Agnese in Agone stands above the arches of the Stadium of Domitian; today's Piazza Navona preserves the shape of the stadium's arena. Ambrose and Pope Damasus already wrote of Agnes's martyrdom; the details come from legend.
The baptism of Fabiola

After Agnes's death Fabiola becomes a Christian. At Easter a small party goes around the city wall to the far side, turns off the Via Portuensis into a vineyard near Caesar's gardens, and goes down into the cemetery of Pontianus, where the two Persian martyrs Abdon and Sennen rest (Part II, chapter 34).

Deep in the catacomb, Fabiola is baptized in a square basin, four to five feet deep, filled from an underground spring. The novel notes that the baptistery still exists, with a painting of the Baptism of Christ above it, added a century or two later.

The catacomb of Pontianus is on the slope of Monteverde; its baptistery and wall paintings can still be seen.
The tomb of Agnes on the Via Nomentana

Agnes's villa lay along the Via Nomentana, a mile and a half from the city; here the novel shows Agnes among her gentle animals. Here Fulvius asks for her hand, and Agnes answers that she is already betrothed (Part II, chapter 12). Agnes is buried in the cemetery beneath the villa. As heir to the villa, Fabiola moves here with the sick Miriam, her former slave Syra, who dies here (Part II, chapter 34).

At the end of the novel, after Constantine's victory, building is already under way in the villa's garden: Constantia, the emperor's daughter, is having a basilica built over Agnes's tomb. Fabiola keeps a hospital in her town house and lives at her villa; Torquatus, now converted, becomes the gravedigger of the villa's cemetery (Part III, chapters 1–3).

Sant'Agnese fuori le Mura and the round Santa Costanza beside it stand beyond the Porta Pia, outside the edge of the map. The old basilica was built in the mid-4th century by Constantina, Constantine's daughter; the novel calls her Constantia.
